A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EISP research work, despite substantial changes to the title, method and framing. All 22 pages of v3 and 28 pages of v4, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables and figures supporting comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original reconstruction experiments on synthetic and real measurements, numerical comparisons in Table 2, ablations, statistical summaries and qualitative 3D results.

after.justification: v4 reports original reconstruction results in Table 1, noise and training-data ablations, quantitative 3D evaluations in Section 5.4, and additional appendix results.

M1.justification: v3 uses transmitter-specific current estimators, analytical current-to-permittivity solvers and averaging across transmitters, trained with current, permittivity and scattering losses. v4 replaces this pipeline with an MLP that directly predicts permittivity from coordinates and concatenated measurements from all transmitters, using only permittivity supervision.

E1.justification: Circular, MNIST, IF, 3D MNIST and 3D ShapeNet remain, with the same reconstruction tasks. Input-condition coverage changes modestly: v4 adds intermediate measurement-noise levels of 10%, 15%, 20% and 25%, while dropping the MNIST transmitter-count sweep at N=4, 8 and 12. Its numerical 3D results concern already covered tasks.

E2.justification: Matched 2D comparisons retain BP, 2-fold SOM, Gs SOM, BPS, PGAN, Physics-Net and Img-Interiors, with 2-fold SOM absent from IF in both. The 3D comparator remains Img-Interiors. Revised scores and the expanded baseline schematic do not establish an actual change to the evaluated baseline procedure.

E3.justification: The reported Circular training set decreases from 60k to 10k examples. Appendix B.3 in v3 versus C.3 in v4 changes MLP width from 256 to 512, training from 300 to 200 iterations, and a decaying learning rate to a constant rate. v4 also introduces training-data-fraction experiments and quantitative 3D evaluation using MSE and IoU.

E4.justification: v3's transmitter-count and three-loss ablations, including their appendix visualizations, are removed. v4 instead tests six noise levels and four training-data fractions, with corresponding tables and qualitative results. New Figure 2 analyzes baseline failures, including an Img-Interiors reconstruction whose simulated field matches measurements despite incorrect object structure.

E5.justification: v3 Appendix C.1/Table 5 and v4 Appendix D.1/Table 4 both describe three independent trials with scaled Gaussian noise and report means and standard deviations. No change to run counts, uncertainty-estimation practices or significance-testing procedures is documented; the numerical summaries change.

E6.justification: Between v3 Table 2 and v4 Table 1, MNIST at 5% noise changes from MSE 0.055 to 0.039 for Ours at N=16 and from 0.079 to 0.085 at N=1; Img-Interiors at N=1 changes from 0.422 to 0.305. Architecture and training changes prevent interpreting these as controlled gains. v4 adds 3D MSE/IoU and new ablation results, updates qualitative reconstructions and statistical values, and changes Figure 1's reported 2D inference time from 0.0016 to 0.0071 seconds.

T1.justification: The forward scattering equations and appendix integral/discrete physical models are retained. v4 removes the short current-to-permittivity derivation in v3 Equation 5 and the associated one-to-one and well-posed transmission arguments. No replacement theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion replace the claimed contribution of a physics-driven, two-stage decomposition using induced current with direct data-driven inversion using learned distribution priors. The title shifts to single-transmitter reconstruction. Fast inference and strong sparse-transmitter reconstruction remain central claims, but the claimed mechanism and principal methodological contribution change substantially.

C2.justification: v4 attributes reconstruction success to learned priors compensating for missing measurements, replacing v3's induced-current and physics-decoupling explanation. It adds an ambiguity-based explanation for converged but incorrect baseline reconstructions and discusses stronger training-data dependence under noise. The limitation changes from unexplored transmitter placement to explicitly being unable to handle different transmitter or receiver locations.

D1.justification: v4 newly documents real/imaginary measurement packing and pooling datasets with identical acquisition settings. Its implementation appendix revises network and training parameters and no longer specifies v3's output tanh, gradient clipping or three loss weights. PyTorch, V100 hardware, the reconstruction grid, positional-encoding frequency and project-page access remain documented.

R1.justification: The contribution is substantially repositioned relative to prior work: v3 emphasizes incorporating scattering physics beyond image-translation methods, whereas v4 emphasizes bypassing BP initialization and learning priors under information scarcity. v4 adds radar/compressive-sensing citations by Baraniuk and Steeghs, Anitori et al., and Leigsnering et al.; it removes v3's physics-inspired CNN citation and two other machine-learning references.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, physical rationale, method description and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. The intermediate-representation subsection disappears, the ablation narrative is replaced, and 3D experiments are consolidated. A new LLM-use appendix shifts the existing appendix labels, while much of the physical-background and dataset prose remains.

P2.justification: Figure 1 and the architecture diagram are substantially redrawn, a new baseline-failure figure is added, and v3's conceptual comparison table is removed. Transmitter/loss-ablation displays are replaced by noise/data-size displays, and numerous reconstruction panels change. The document also adopts different typography, text width and figure/table placement throughout.

improvement.justification: v4 provides clearer support for its revised data-prior explanation through the failure analysis in Figure 2 and training-data ablation, adds quantitative evidence for previously qualitative 3D claims, and states the sensor-location limitation more explicitly. These improve explanatory clarity and empirical support. The gain is limited by removal of the transmitter-count sweep and by simultaneous architecture and training changes that prevent a controlled comparison with v3; higher reported scores alone do not establish improvement.
